y-m-80-01.title: What number goes in the center square of the Nakseo magic square?
y-m-80-01.topic: The structure of the Nakseo (3×3 magic square) and the center square
y-m-80-01.goal: In an arrangement that must satisfy every line with an equal sum, count how many lines each number can take part in to sort out the candidates for the center square, and state the reason.
y-m-80-01.material:
An old Chinese story tells of the 3×3 'Nakseo (洛書)', said to have been found in the pattern on a turtle's back. It is an arrangement in which the numbers 1 to 9 are placed once each in the squares so that the sum of the three numbers is 15 in all 3 rows, 3 columns, and 2 diagonals (8 lines in all). The center square has 4 lines passing through it: 1 row, 1 column, and 2 diagonals.
Yunho said, "There's no rule that says 5 must go in the center. I think you can put 1 in the center and still make all 8 line sums 15."
y-m-80-01.thinking.0: Finding all the cases that satisfy the conditions and making a list
y-m-80-01.thinking.1: Counting the list to judge possible or impossible
y-m-80-01.thinking.2: Refuting the suggestion (1 in the center) with a counterexample
y-m-80-01.prereq.0: Natural numbers from 1 to 9 and addition of three numbers
y-m-80-01.prereq.1: Assumption: Mathematics and Culture is an elective subject, solved by students who have learned up to middle school math. The difficulty marks H1/H2 are only the difficulty of this bundle and not an assignment to a particular grade.
y-m-80-01.s.s1.prompt: Find 4 groups of three different numbers (natural numbers from 1 to 9) whose sum is 15. Groups that differ only in order count as the same group.
y-m-80-01.s.s1.hint.0: Decide the smallest number first, then write what the sum of the other two numbers must be.
y-m-80-01.s.s1.hint.1: Line up the numbers of the groups you found from smallest, and compare to check that you did not write the same group again in a different order.
y-m-80-01.s.s1.ok.c1: All three numbers are natural numbers from 1 to 9.
y-m-80-01.s.s1.fail.c1: All three numbers must be natural numbers from 1 to 9.
y-m-80-01.s.s1.ok.c2: The three numbers are all different.
y-m-80-01.s.s1.fail.c2: A magic square does not use the same number twice. Make the three numbers different from each other.
y-m-80-01.s.s1.ok.c3: The sum of the three numbers is 15.
y-m-80-01.s.s1.fail.c3: The sum of the three numbers is not 15. Check the sum again.
y-m-80-01.s.s1.explain: There are 8 groups of three different numbers whose sum is 15: 1+5+9, 1+6+8, 2+4+9, 2+5+8, 2+6+7, 3+4+8, 3+5+7, 4+5+6. This list is the basis for the next step.
y-m-80-01.s.s2.prompt: The groups with sum 15 are the 8 above and no others. The number that goes in the center square needs 4 groups containing that number, one for each of the row, the column, and the 2 diagonals. How can you judge Yunho's idea (1 in the center)?
y-m-80-01.s.s2.hint.0: Count how many times 1 appears in the 8 groups.
y-m-80-01.s.s2.hint.1: Write how many lines pass through the center square, and compare that number with the count you just made.
y-m-80-01.s.s2.o.a: It is possible. There are groups that contain 1, so among the 4 lines I can make just that group work and fill the rest with other numbers.
y-m-80-01.s.s2.r.a: You thought only one group has to work. The center square belongs to all 4 lines, so all 4 lines must have a sum of 15.
y-m-80-01.s.s2.o.b: I can't tell. I can't judge before checking directly every way of arranging the 8 groups.
y-m-80-01.s.s2.r.b: You thought you wouldn't know without trying every arrangement one by one. Just counting how often a number appears lets you know that no arrangement is possible.
y-m-80-01.s.s2.o.c: It is impossible. There are only 2 groups that contain 1, but the center square has to belong to 4 different groups.
y-m-80-01.s.s2.r.c: This is a thought that judged by comparing the number of groups with the number of lines needed.
y-m-80-01.s.s2.o.d: It is impossible. 1 is odd, but only even numbers can go in the center square.
y-m-80-01.s.s2.r.d: The reasoning is different. 5 is also odd, and there is no rule that the center square must be even.
y-m-80-01.s.s2.explain: There are only two groups containing 1, (1,5,9) and (1,6,8), but 4 lines pass through the center square, so not all 4 lines can include 1. On the other hand, there are four groups containing 5: (1,5,9), (2,5,8), (3,5,7), (4,5,6).
y-m-80-01.s.s3.prompt: Choose a number other than 5 for the center square (one of 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9), and explain to Yunho, using the 8 groups, why that number can't be the center square.
y-m-80-01.s.s3.hint.0: Find in the 8 groups the groups that contain your chosen number and count them.
y-m-80-01.s.s3.hint.1: Write as a sentence the result of comparing that count with the number of lines passing through the center square.
y-m-80-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you count the groups containing your chosen number yourself?
y-m-80-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you use the fact that 4 lines pass through the center square?
y-m-80-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you check once more that the same method works for other numbers?
y-m-80-01.s.s3.model.0: If 8 were in the center, there are only three groups with 8, (1,6,8), (2,5,8), (3,4,8), so I can't fill the 4 lines. So 8 is not allowed.
y-m-80-01.s.s3.model.1: If the center number is x, the sum of the 4 lines through the center is 60. The 4 lines count the center 4 times and the other 8 squares once each, so 60=45+3x, and x=5. So only 5 is possible.
y-m-80-01.s.s3.modelNote.1: This is another method that explains with an equation instead of counting groups.

y-m-80-02.title: Which area does a '34 pyeong type' ad refer to?
y-m-80-02.topic: The area unit pyeong and ㎡, supply area and exclusive area
y-m-80-02.goal: Check whether the result of a unit conversion is realistic, know that the same 'pyeong' label can point to different areas, point out the information needed, and rewrite the label.
y-m-80-02.material:
This is a fictional apartment sales notice.
"하늘마을 34-pyeong type: supply area 112㎡, exclusive area 84㎡"
Unit relationship: 1 pyeong is about 3.3058㎡ (exactly 400/121㎡).
Seoha looked at the notice and said, "I converted the exclusive area of 84㎡ to pyeong and it doesn't seem like 34 pyeong. Isn't the ad wrong?" Dad said, "The 34 pyeong is the supply area converted to pyeong." Seoha calculated as below (approximating 1 pyeong as 3.3㎡).
y-m-80-02.thinking.0: Checking the direction of the conversion and whether the result is realistic
y-m-80-02.thinking.1: Sorting out what information is needed for a judgment
y-m-80-02.thinking.2: Rewriting the label so readers are not misled
y-m-80-02.prereq.0: The area of a rectangle and the unit ㎡
y-m-80-02.prereq.1: Calculations with decimals (calculators may be used)
y-m-80-02.prereq.2: Assumption: Mathematics and Culture is an elective subject, solved by students who have learned up to middle school math. The difficulty marks H1/H2 are only the difficulty of this bundle and not an assignment to a particular grade.
y-m-80-02.s.s1.prompt: Choose one strange line in Seoha's calculation.
y-m-80-02.s.s1.hint.0: Think about how big a home 84㎡ is, and compare whether 277 pyeong is that big.
y-m-80-02.s.s1.hint.1: If ㎡ fits 3.3 times into 1 pyeong, work out whether the number of pyeong in 84㎡ would be more or less.
y-m-80-02.s.s1.line.1: To convert the exclusive area of 84㎡ to pyeong, I calculated 84×3.3 = 277.2.
y-m-80-02.s.s1.line.2: Therefore the exclusive area is about 277 pyeong.
y-m-80-02.s.s1.line.3: 34 pyeong and 277 pyeong are too different, so the ad is wrong.
y-m-80-02.s.s1.explain: Seoha's calculation went in the wrong direction in line 2. If 1 pyeong is 3.3㎡, the number of pyeong should be smaller than the number of ㎡, but 277, much larger than 84, came out. Lines 3 and 4 are the result of trusting that value as it is. If you first check whether the converted value is realistic (can 84㎡ be 277 pyeong?), you can spot the mistake. (84÷3.3 ≈ 25.5 pyeong)
y-m-80-02.s.s2.prompt: To judge whether the ad's '34 pyeong type' is wrong, what should you check first in the notice?
y-m-80-02.s.s2.hint.0: Count how many area numbers appear in the notice.
y-m-80-02.s.s2.hint.1: Convert each area to pyeong and compare which area is closer to 34.
y-m-80-02.s.s2.o.a: Which floor of the building the 34 pyeong type is on
y-m-80-02.s.s2.r.a: The floor number does not decide the size of the area. The information needed is the kind of area.
y-m-80-02.s.s2.o.b: Whether 1 pyeong is 3.3㎡ or 3.3058㎡, that is, to how many decimal places the value is exact
y-m-80-02.s.s2.r.b: Whether you divide 112㎡ by 3.3 or by 3.3058, it is close to 34 pyeong. The difference in the approximation does not change the conclusion.
y-m-80-02.s.s2.r.c: Even if you know the price, you can't know which area the '34 pyeong' is a converted value of.
y-m-80-02.s.s2.o.d: Which area, supply or exclusive, the 34 pyeong is the converted value of
y-m-80-02.s.s2.r.d: This is the idea of checking the kind of area the label points to.
y-m-80-02.s.s2.explain: The same home has both a supply area (112㎡) and an exclusive area (84㎡), so you need to know which area the label converted into pyeong to judge whether it is wrong or right. 112÷3.3058 ≈ 33.9 pyeong (about 34 pyeong), and 84÷3.3058 ≈ 25.4 pyeong.
y-m-80-02.s.s3.prompt: Write a reply to Seoha. Write the values of the supply area and the exclusive area each converted to pyeong, and also suggest one way to rewrite the notice's '34 pyeong type' label so there is less misunderstanding.
y-m-80-02.s.s3.hint.0: Divide 84㎡ and 112㎡ each by the area corresponding to 1 pyeong to find the number of pyeong.
y-m-80-02.s.s3.hint.1: Write what words, added before or after 'pyeong' in the ad phrase, would show which area it is.
y-m-80-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you check that the values of the two areas converted to pyeong are realistic sizes?
y-m-80-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you explain why Seoha's first doubt was a wrong conclusion (or how far it was right)?
y-m-80-02.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Does the label you proposed really reduce the reader's misunderstanding?
y-m-80-02.s.s3.model.0: Seoha, the exclusive area of 84㎡ is about 25.4 pyeong and the supply area of 112㎡ is about 33.9 pyeong. The ad's 34 pyeong is the converted supply area, so it isn't wrong. I'd like the ad to also say which area it is, like 'supply area 112㎡ (about 34 pyeong)'.
y-m-80-02.s.s3.model.1: Dividing 84 by 3.3 gives about 25 pyeong, which is how big the exclusive area is, and 112㎡ is about 34 pyeong, so the ad is based on the supply area. If you write the kind of area together with the ㎡ value, there's no confusion. It was good that you doubted, but it was a pity you looked only at the exclusive area.

y-m-80-03.title: Is a triangle made with a 12-segment knotted rope always a right triangle?
y-m-80-03.topic: A knotted rope that makes a right angle and the conditions for the Pythagorean theorem
y-m-80-03.goal: Know that one successful example does not guarantee a generalization, make a triangle that meets the condition (12 segments around) but is not a right triangle, and state the correct criterion for deciding whether it is a right angle.
y-m-80-03.material:
It is said that in the old days people marked 12 segments on a rope with equally spaced knots to make a right angle. You join the two ends of the rope into a loop and make three sides that bend at the knots. The number of segments in each side is a natural number, and the sum of the three sides is 12 segments. (For the three sides to form a triangle, the longest side must be shorter than the sum of the other two.)
Doyun said, "I tried 3 segments, 4 segments, and 5 segments and it made a right angle. So a triangle made from a 12-segment rope is always a right triangle!"
y-m-80-03.thinking.0: Evaluating whether one example can be generalized
y-m-80-03.thinking.1: Making a counterexample yourself that fits the conditions
y-m-80-03.thinking.2: Stating the criterion for deciding that it is a right angle
y-m-80-03.prereq.0: In a right triangle, the relationship between the sum of the squares of two sides and the square of the longest side (a topic of middle school math)
y-m-80-03.prereq.1: The condition for a triangle to be formed (the longest side is shorter than the sum of the other two)
y-m-80-03.prereq.2: Assumption: Mathematics and Culture is an elective subject, solved by students who have learned up to middle school math. The difficulty marks H1/H2 are only the difficulty of this bundle and not an assignment to a particular grade.
y-m-80-03.s.s1.prompt: From Doyun's evidence alone, can we say 'a triangle made from a 12-segment rope is always a right angle'?
y-m-80-03.s.s1.hint.0: Count how many triangles Doyun tested.
y-m-80-03.s.s1.hint.1: Besides 3, 4, 5, find and write other three natural numbers whose sum is 12.
y-m-80-03.s.s1.o.a: We can say it. There is one example that actually became a right angle, so the rule is right.
y-m-80-03.s.s1.r.a: You took the fact that there is one example that fits as proof that the whole rule is right.
y-m-80-03.s.s1.o.b: We can't say it. We also need to test other triangles made with 12 segments.
y-m-80-03.s.s1.r.b: This is the idea of testing other cases of the same condition before trusting a generalization.
y-m-80-03.s.s1.o.c: We can say it. If the rope length is the same, the shape of the triangle made is the same too.
y-m-80-03.s.s1.r.c: You thought that if the perimeter is the same, the shape is the same. Test whether different shapes can come out with the same perimeter.
y-m-80-03.s.s1.o.d: We can't say it. A triangle becoming a right angle is chance, so we can't state it as a rule.
y-m-80-03.s.s1.r.d: You missed that there is a reason when it becomes a right angle. You need to sort out the cases that can be written as a rule from those that cannot.
y-m-80-03.s.s1.explain: To show 'always', it has to be right in every case, and to break it, one counterexample is enough. 3, 4, 5 is just an example that fits, and the other triangles of 12 segments have not been tested yet.
y-m-80-03.s.s2.prompt: Find a triangle that breaks Doyun's statement. The numbers of segments of the three sides are natural numbers, their sum is 12, and make 2 triangles of different shapes that are triangles but not right triangles. (Ones that differ only in order are the same triangle.)
y-m-80-03.s.s2.hint.0: Starting from the smallest number, list all sets of three natural numbers whose sum is 12.
y-m-80-03.s.s2.hint.1: From your list, keep only the ones where the longest side is shorter than the sum of the other two, and pick ones that are not 3, 4, 5.
y-m-80-03.s.s2.ok.c1: The three sides are natural numbers.
y-m-80-03.s.s2.fail.c1: The three sides must be natural numbers that are at least 1.
y-m-80-03.s.s2.ok.c2: The sum of the three sides is 12.
y-m-80-03.s.s2.fail.c2: The sum of the three sides is not 12.
y-m-80-03.s.s2.ok.c3: The longest side is shorter than the sum of the other two, so it forms a triangle.
y-m-80-03.s.s2.fail.c3: Check whether the longest side is shorter than the sum of the other two. A triangle cannot be made with these lengths.
y-m-80-03.s.s2.ok.c4: It is not a right triangle. It is an example that breaks Doyun's statement.
y-m-80-03.s.s2.fail.c4: This triangle is a right triangle. You need to find a triangle that is not a right angle.
y-m-80-03.s.s2.explain: The sets of natural numbers with sum 12 that form a triangle are only three: (2,5,5), (3,4,5), (4,4,4). Of these only (3,4,5) is a right angle and the other two are not. So Doyun's statement does not hold.
y-m-80-03.s.s3.prompt: What would you like to tell Doyun? Use the side lengths of the triangle you just found to show that it is not 'always a right angle', and also write what you need to check to find out which triangles are right triangles.
y-m-80-03.s.s3.hint.0: Write the squares of each of the three sides of the triangle you just made.
y-m-80-03.s.s3.hint.1: Compare the square of the longest side with the sum of the squares of the other two sides.
y-m-80-03.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you check that the triangle I gave really has a sum of 12?
y-m-80-03.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Is it clear that you did not deny '3, 4, 5 is a right angle' but broke the word 'always'?
y-m-80-03.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you state the criterion for deciding a right angle in terms of side lengths?
y-m-80-03.s.s3.model.0: No. If you bend the rope with 4 segments, 4 segments, 4 segments, it is 12 segments, but it is an equilateral triangle, so there is no right angle. To know whether it is a right angle, you have to check whether the square of the longest side equals the sum of the squares of the other two.
y-m-80-03.s.s3.model.1: If you bend the rope with 2, 5, 5, the sum is 12 segments too. But 2²+5²=29 and 5²=25, so it is not a right angle. You can't tell a right angle from the rope length alone, and you have to examine the squares of the three sides.

y-m-80-04.title: How large is 8㎠ on a map in reality?
y-m-80-04.topic: Map scale and the real size of an area
y-m-80-04.goal: Use the fact that the ratio of lengths and the ratio of areas are different to find the mistake in a map solution, make rectangles on a map in several ways that fit the conditions, and judge how the area changes when the scale changes.
y-m-80-04.material: When the park in front of City Hall was drawn on a map with a scale of 1:25000, it was a rectangle, 4cm wide and 2cm tall on the map. (1:25000 means 1cm on the map is 25000cm in reality, that is, 250m.) Seoa wrote a solution that finds the real area of the park.
y-m-80-04.thinking.0: Finding contradictions between the lines of the working
y-m-80-04.thinking.1: Making several designs that satisfy the conditions
y-m-80-04.thinking.2: Judging that length and area change differently when the scale changes
y-m-80-04.prereq.0: The meaning of scale (the ratio of length on the map to real length)
y-m-80-04.prereq.2: The relationship between cm, m, and km
y-m-80-04.prereq.3: Assumption: Mathematics and Culture is an elective subject, solved by students who have learned up to middle school math. The difficulty marks H1/H2 are only the difficulty of this bundle and not an assignment to a particular grade.
y-m-80-04.s.s1.prompt: Choose the wrong line in Seoa's working. If there are lines that contradict each other, you may choose either one of them.
y-m-80-04.s.s1.hint.0: Multiply the real width and height found in lines 2 and 3, and compare the result with the value in line 5.
y-m-80-04.s.s1.hint.1: Write how many m by how many m a 1cm×1cm square on the map is in reality, and work out whether its area is 25000 times as large.
y-m-80-04.s.s1.line.0: 1cm on the map is 25000cm in reality.
y-m-80-04.s.s1.line.3: The area of the park on the map is 4×2 = 8cm².
y-m-80-04.s.s1.line.4: The real area is 8cm² multiplied by 25000, which is 200000cm² = 20m².
y-m-80-04.s.s1.line.5: Therefore the park, 1000m wide and 500m tall, has an area of 20m².
y-m-80-04.s.s1.explain: Line 5 is wrong. Lengths become 25000 times as large, but for the area, both width and height become 25000 times as large, so the area becomes 25000×25000 times (625000000 times). 8cm²×625000000 = 5000000000cm² = 500000m² = 0.5km². Line 6 contradicts the earlier lines, since multiplying the width of 1000m and the height of 500m in lines 2 and 3 should give 500000m².
y-m-80-04.s.s2.prompt: The real area of this park is 0.5km². Find 3 pairs of width a (cm) and height b (cm) with different shapes that are possible when drawn as a rectangle on a map of the same scale (1:25000). (The map has each side within 40cm, and a width and height swapped in order count as the same shape.)
y-m-80-04.s.s2.hint.0: Change 0.5km² into m² or cm², and divide by how many real cm² 1cm² on the map is.
y-m-80-04.s.s2.hint.1: Decide what the area on the map should be, then write several pairs of two numbers whose product is that value.
y-m-80-04.s.s2.ok.c1: The size fits on the map.
y-m-80-04.s.s2.fail.c1: a and b must be greater than 0 and at most 40cm.
y-m-80-04.s.s2.ok.c2: The area on the map is 8cm², so the real area is 0.5km².
y-m-80-04.s.s2.fail.c2: The area on the map is different. First find how many cm² the real area of 0.5km² is on the map.
y-m-80-04.s.s2.explain: If the real area is 0.5km², the area on the map is 8cm². The product of the width and height just has to be 8. (4,2), (8,1), (5,1.6), and so on are all possible. This condition alone does not fix a single shape for the park.
y-m-80-04.s.s3.prompt: If the same park is drawn on a map with a scale of 1:50000 (the map's width and height become half those of the first map), what will the area of the park on the map be?
y-m-80-04.s.s3.hint.0: Write the park's width and height from the first map each reduced to half, and multiply them yourself.
y-m-80-04.s.s3.hint.1: Compare with the area on the first map and calculate what fraction it is.
y-m-80-04.s.s3.o.a: It becomes one quarter of the first, 2cm².
y-m-80-04.s.s3.r.a: This is a thought that reflects that both width and height become half, so the area changes by a product.
y-m-80-04.s.s3.o.b: It becomes half of the first map, 4cm².
y-m-80-04.s.s3.r.b: You thought that if the length is half, the area is half too. Find yourself the area of a rectangle whose width and height are both half.
y-m-80-04.s.s3.o.c: It is 8cm², the same as at first.
y-m-80-04.s.s3.r.c: You thought that since the real size is the same, the area on the map is the same. When the scale changes, the lengths on the map change.
y-m-80-04.s.s3.o.d: It becomes twice the first map, 16cm².
y-m-80-04.s.s3.r.d: You thought that when the number of the scale gets bigger, the picture on the map gets bigger too. 1:50000 is a map drawn smaller than 1:25000.
y-m-80-04.s.s3.explain: If the width of 4cm and height of 2cm each become half, they are 2cm and 1cm, and the area is 2cm². When the lengths become half, the area becomes one quarter.

y-m-80-05.title: If you pair 10 heavenly stems with 12 earthly branches, after how many years does the same name come around?
y-m-80-05.topic: The cycle of the sixty ganji made by the heavenly stems and earthly branches
y-m-80-05.goal: Check and fix the first estimate (all 120 names are used) with new data, make the pairs that are not used yourself, and explain why the cycle is 60 years through the relationship of the two cycles.
y-m-80-05.material:
The old calendar gave each year a name called 'ganji'. The 10 heavenly stems (갑 을 병 정 무 기 경 신 임 계) and the 12 earthly branches (자 축 인 묘 진 사 오 미 신 유 술 해) are each cycled in order and paired one for each year, so the names move one step each year: 갑자, 을축, 병인, 정묘, ... When the stems end, it goes back to 갑, and when the branches end, it goes back to 자. The numbers are 갑=1, 을=2, ..., 계=10, 자=1, 축=2, ..., 해=12.
Minseo said, "There are 10×12=120 names, so it will come back to the first name 갑자 only after using up all 120 names."
y-m-80-05.thinking.0: Revising your judgment while looking at the data one piece at a time
y-m-80-05.thinking.1: Making a pair that is not used yourself and using it as a counterexample
y-m-80-05.thinking.2: Explaining when two cycles come back together
y-m-80-05.prereq.0: Multiples and common multiples of natural numbers
y-m-80-05.prereq.2: Assumption: Mathematics and Culture is an elective subject, solved by students who have learned up to middle school math. The difficulty marks H1/H2 are only the difficulty of this bundle and not an assignment to a particular grade.
y-m-80-05.s.s1.prompt: Judge whether Minseo's statement is right while looking at the data one piece at a time.
y-m-80-05.s.s1.hint.0: Write the names for years 1 to 13 in a table and mark the years when 갑 appears.
y-m-80-05.s.s1.hint.1: For each year when 갑 appeared, write the branch number of that year next to it.

y-m-80-06.title: Is the rule 'a year divisible by 4 is a leap year' always right?
y-m-80-06.topic: The leap year rule of the Gregorian calendar and the length of an average year
y-m-80-06.goal: Know that a few years matching a rule does not guarantee the whole rule, find the years where the rule breaks yourself, and judge by calculating how the exception rules change the length of an average year.
y-m-80-06.material:
In the calendar we use (the Gregorian calendar), a leap year is a year in which February has 29 days. The rule is: ① A year divisible by 4 is a leap year. ② Of those, a year divisible by 100 is not a leap year (a common year). ③ Of those, a year divisible by 400 is a leap year again.
Jia did not know rules ② and ③ and said, "A year divisible by 4 is a leap year. 2020, 2024, and 2028 are all leap years. So this rule is always right!"

y-m-80-06.s.s2.explain: In this period, the years where Jia's rule is wrong are 1700, 1800, 1900, 2100, 2200, and 2300. 2000, 1600, and 2400 are divisible by 400, so they are leap years again.
y-m-80-06.s.s3.prompt: With the rules above, how many leap years are there in total over 400 years (for example, from 1601 to 2000)? With this value, the length of an average year is 365 + (number of leap years ÷ 400) days. (If you use only Jia's rule, it is 100 in 400 years.)
y-m-80-06.s.s3.hint.0: Find the number of multiples of 4, multiples of 100, and multiples of 400 in 400 years.

y-m-80-06.s.s3.r.a: This is the result of counting all multiples of 4 as leap years. Multiples of 100 have to be removed as common years.
y-m-80-06.s.s3.r.b: You counted by subtracting the multiples of 100 from the multiples of 4 and adding back the multiples of 400.
y-m-80-06.s.s3.r.c: You subtracted the multiples of 100 as common years but did not reflect that the multiples of 400 become leap years again.

y-m-80-06.s.s3.explain: In 400 years, there are 100 multiples of 4, of which 4 are multiples of 100 (and of those, 1 is a multiple of 400). 100−4+1=97. The average year is 365+97/400=365.2425 days, which is closer to the actual about 365.2422 days than Jia's rule (365.25 days).

y-m-80-07.title: Why does multiplying by halving and doubling work?
y-m-80-07.topic: The principle of an old multiplication method (multiplying by halving and doubling)
y-m-80-07.goal: Find the line where the rule was applied wrongly in the working of the old multiplication method, and use the reason the rule works (the left number is split into a sum of powers of 2) to make a starting number that fits the conditions yourself and explain it.
y-m-80-07.material:
This is a multiplication method that was used in many places in the old days. Write the two numbers A and B to be multiplied in two columns. On the left, start from A and keep halving (dropping the remainder) until you reach 1, and on the right, start from B and keep doubling. Keep only the rows where the left number is odd, and add up all the right numbers in those rows to get A×B.
Example: 23×14
Left 23, right 14 (odd row)
Left 11, right 28 (odd row)
Left 5, right 56 (odd row)
Left 2, right 112 (even row)
Left 1, right 224 (odd row)
14+28+56+224 = 322 = 23×14
Seoyun tried to solve 26×15 with this method.

A=7 gives 7, 3, 1, which is 3 rows, so it doesn't work, and A=8 gives 8, 4, 2, 1, with only 1 row. When A is the sum of two powers of 2, there are 2 rows (3=1+2, 5=1+4, 6=2+4, 9=1+8).

y-m-80-08.material:
It is known that when A4 copy paper is cut in half at the middle of its long side it becomes A5 of the same shape, and two sheets of A3 have the same shape as one sheet of A2. Here 'the same shape' means the two rectangles are similar, that is, the ratio of the long side to the short side is the same. (Long side l and short side w of the rectangle, in mm)

y-m-80-09.title: If there is a check digit, can it catch every typing mistake?
y-m-80-09.topic: The check digit of a book number (ISBN) and detecting errors
y-m-80-09.goal: Check with examples which kinds of input mistakes a check digit is sure to catch and which it can miss, and explain its limit by making a case it misses yourself.
y-m-80-09.material:
The International Standard Book Number (ISBN-13) on a book's back cover is 13 digits. Multiply the first 12 digits in turn by 1, 3, 1, 3, ... and add them all up to get S, and the 13th digit (the check digit) is the digit from 0 to 9 that makes the total a multiple of 10 when added to S.
Example (a made-up number): if the first 12 digits are 9 7 8 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9, then S = 9×1+7×3+8×1+1×3+2×1+3×3+4×1+5×3+6×1+7×3+8×1+9×3 = 133, and the check digit is 7 (133+7=140).
Seojin said, "Since there is a check digit, if you type the number wrong, it can catch every mistake!"

y-m-80-11.title: If you stack 12 fifths, do you get exactly octaves?
y-m-80-11.topic: Musical scales and powers: do stacked perfect fifths meet the octave?
y-m-80-11.goal: Compare the sizes of powers to show that the claim '12 fifths = 7 octaves' does not hold exactly, understand the odd-even argument that explains this briefly, and compare two directions of solution in instrument making.
y-m-80-11.material:
The pitch of a sound can be expressed by frequency, and the relationship of two pitches is compared by the ratio of their frequencies. In old theory, a 'perfect fifth' has a frequency ratio of 3:2 (the upper note is 1.5 times), and raising a note by one octave doubles its frequency. Some people believed that if you stack 12 perfect fifths up from a note, you pass through all 12 notes and return to the same note 7 octaves higher.
Seou said, "(3/2) multiplied 12 times will be exactly equal to 2 multiplied 7 times. Then the keyboard closes up perfectly." (3/2 is three halves, and 2⁷ is 2 multiplied 7 times, which is 128)

y-m-80-11.s.s2.r.d: You used the facts that odd times odd is odd, and a number multiplied by 2 is even.

This argument does not need calculation, and it applies the same way not just to 12 but to any number of stackings.

y-m-80-11.s.s3.model.0: If you keep the fifth pure (3:2), the chords are clear, but the note stacked 12 times is off from 7 octaves by about 1.4%, so there are intervals that are hard to use. In 12-tone equal temperament every fifth is narrowed a little to share this mismatch, so it can be used in any key, but the chords are not pure.
y-m-80-11.s.s3.model.1: Equal temperament reduces each fifth by about 2 cents so that 12 of them make exactly 7 octaves. In exchange, every fifth departs a little from the pure 3:2. Pure fifths sound clear, but they have the downside that when you stack 12, the mismatch piles up in one place.

y-m-80-12.title: How often must a leap month be added to keep in step with the seasons?
y-m-80-12.topic: The leap month rule of the lunar calendar and the Metonic cycle
y-m-80-12.goal: Using the fact that the Moon's month (about 29.53 days) and the year (about 365.24 days) are not whole-number multiples of each other, estimate the proportion of leap months, compare how much error builds up, and choose a better rule with reasons.
y-m-80-12.material:
The lunar calendar takes one cycle of the Moon's shape (about 29.53059 days) as one month. The seasons, on the other hand, must match the year it takes to go around the Sun (about 365.2422 days). 12 months is 12×29.53059≈354.367 days, which is about 10.9 days short each year. So a month is added every few years, called a 'leap month'. If a leap month is added k times in n years, the number of days in the calendar is (12n+k)×29.53059, and the number of days of the seasons is n×365.2422.
Minjae said, "If we add a leap month once every 3 years, it will match well enough."

y-m-80-13.title: How many different arrangements can there be on a Go board?
y-m-80-13.topic: Counting cases on a Go board and estimating huge numbers
y-m-80-13.goal: Know that when the choice at each intersection is independent the number of cases grows by multiplying, not adding, estimate the size of a very large power from above and below, and explain that some arrangements cannot occur in a real game because of the rules.
y-m-80-13.material:
The points where the 19 horizontal lines and 19 vertical lines of a Go board meet number 19×19=361. Each point is in one of 3 states: 'empty', 'a black stone is placed', or 'a white stone is placed'. The rules of Go: Black and white take turns placing one stone at a time, and a stone is removed from the board (captured) if it has no neighboring empty point (liberty) up, down, left, or right.
Junho calculated 'the number of arrangements that can appear on a Go board' like this.
y-m-80-13.thinking.0: Finding the error in a solution that counts cases
y-m-80-13.thinking.1: Estimating a large number from above and below
y-m-80-13.thinking.2: Distinguishing possible arrangements from arrangements that can occur
y-m-80-13.prereq.0: The number of cases (the multiplication rule)
y-m-80-13.prereq.2: The basic rules of Go (liberties, capture)
y-m-80-13.prereq.3: Assumption: Mathematics and Culture is an elective subject, solved by students who have learned up to middle school math. The difficulty marks H1/H2 are only the difficulty of this bundle and not an assignment to a particular grade.
y-m-80-13.s.s1.prompt: Choose the wrong line in Junho's working. If there are lines that are linked to each other, you may choose any one of them.
y-m-80-13.s.s1.hint.0: Write all the possible arrangements on a very small board with 2 points.
y-m-80-13.s.s1.hint.1: Count the number of arrangements when there are 3 points, and observe how the count changes when one more point is added.
y-m-80-13.s.s1.line.1: Each point is in one of 3 states: empty, black stone, or white stone.
y-m-80-13.s.s1.line.2: Each point has 3 options, so adding up the cases for all the points gives 3+3+…+3 = 3×361 = 1083 cases.
y-m-80-13.s.s1.line.3: Therefore there are 1083 arrangements on the Go board.
y-m-80-13.s.s1.explain: Line 3 is wrong. The choices at the points are independent of each other, so you multiply the number of cases rather than add them. With 2 points it is 3×3=9, with 3 points it is 3×3×3=27, and with 361 points it is 3^361, that is, 3 multiplied 361 times. Line 4 is the wrong conclusion that follows from it.
y-m-80-13.s.s2.prompt: If you fix the working above, the number of arrangements is 3^361, the number you get by multiplying 3 by itself 361 times. Let's estimate its size. 3 multiplied 21 times is 10460353203 (about 1.05×10^10), and 361 = 21×17 + 4. In what range is 3^361?
y-m-80-13.s.s2.hint.0: Compare whether 3^21 is greater or less than 10^10, and write what power of 10 it exceeds when multiplied 17 times.
y-m-80-13.s.s2.hint.1: Estimate 3^21 as 1.05×10^10 and check the size of multiplying it 17 times from above as well.
y-m-80-13.s.s2.r.a: You estimated from above and below by multiplying 3^21 seventeen times and then by 3^4.
y-m-80-13.s.s2.r.b: Since 3^21 exceeds 10^10, multiplying 17 times exceeds 10^170. This estimate is much smaller than that.
y-m-80-13.s.s2.r.c: Since 3^21 exceeds 10^10, multiplying 17 times exceeds 10^170. This estimate is smaller than that.
y-m-80-13.s.s2.r.d: If you multiply 17 times knowing 3^21 is less than 1.05×10^10, it does not exceed 10^173. This upper estimate is too big.
y-m-80-13.s.s3.prompt: Among the 3^361 arrangements, some cannot occur in a real Go game (the number of arrangements that can actually occur is known to be about 2.08×10^170). Give one arrangement that cannot occur and explain why.
y-m-80-13.s.s3.hint.0: Think, in light of the rules, about whether a stone on the board can remain with no liberties.
y-m-80-13.s.s3.hint.1: For the arrangement you thought of, work backward to what the board looked like just before the last move.
y-m-80-13.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you think about whether the arrangement I gave really can't occur because of the rules (impossible by whatever order it is made)?
y-m-80-13.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you distinguish the difference between 'possible arrangements' and 'arrangements that actually occur'?
y-m-80-13.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you write knowing that one counterexample is enough?
y-m-80-13.s.s3.model.0: An arrangement where the whole board is filled with black stones only can't occur. The last black stone placed would have no liberties and also would not capture an opponent's stone, so it can't be played.
y-m-80-13.s.s3.model.1: An arrangement where one black stone remains on the board with all four sides blocked by white stones can't occur. A stone with no liberties is captured and disappears from the board, so such an arrangement does not arise during a game.
